items.text: For a status, use badge with a subtle fill, an icon and a word. Don't use a full-strength fill. Subtle fills let many statuses share one table.
For a supporting text, use type.caption. Don't use type.body. Timestamps and hints step back, so the values stay the hero.
For a text in a table cell, use type.data. Don't use type.body. Every cell shares the mono face, so IDs, times and values line up down each column.
Badge's neutral tone. New and False positive: not triaged yet, or a finished outcome that is not a failure.
Badge's info tone. Investigating: an analyst is on it; news, nothing to act on.
Badge's success tone. Resolved: contained and closed.
Badge's warning tone. Escalated: needs a senior analyst soon, still containable.
Badge's danger tone. Breach confirmed: a real loss.

items.text: For a page title, use type.title. Don't use type.display. Titles stay small so the table starts higher on the screen.
Between page sections, use space.gap.section and a hairline. Don't use a card around every section. Lines separate without taking room from the data.
For a table row height, use size.row (compact). Don't use the comfortable row. Compact rows show more records without scrolling.

For a hero line or key number, use type.display. Don't use type.display for page titles. It is for the one key number at the top of a dashboard. One big total gives analysts the headline at a glance. Everything below it stays small so more rows fit.
For a section heading, use type.heading. Don't use type.title. Panel and card headings sit one step above body. They name a block without taking rows from the data.
For a title of a form page, use type.title. Don't use type.display. Settings and form pages keep the same small title as every page. Experts find the fields higher up.
For a parts of one item, use space.gap.tight. Don't use space.gap.default. An icon and its word sit close, so each item reads as one unit in a dense row.
For a items in a list or a form row, use space.gap.default. Don't use space.gap.tight. Items in a list sit close but apart. Analysts still tell one record from the next.
Between groups, use space.gap.group. Don't use space.gap.section. A small step marks a new group without pushing records off the screen.
Inside a button or input, use space.inset.control-x. Don't use padding set by eye. Narrow padding keeps buttons short, so a toolbar holds every action an expert repeats.
Inside a card, panel or dialog, use space.inset.container. Don't use space.gap.section. Cards and dialogs keep a small inset, so their content starts close to the edge.
Inside a table cell, use space.inset.cell-x. Don't use space.inset.container. Narrow cell padding fits more columns, and values in two columns still stay apart.
For a something that grows past one line, use radius.element. Don't use radius.surface. Rows and text areas keep the small control corner, so long lists stay straight.
For a corners of cards, menus and dialogs, use radius.surface. Don't use radius.control. Cards and menus get a corner just softer than controls. Panels still tile neatly on a busy screen.
For a edges and dividers, use border-width.default. Don't use a thicker border. A hairline separates rows and cards without taking room from the data.
For a most buttons and inputs, use size.control.default. Don't use size.control.large. Buttons and inputs fit a mouse and keep toolbars short.

For the main action on a screen, use size.control.large. Don't use a taller button for the main action. It is the same height as the default here. Color and place mark the main action. One height keeps toolbar buttons in line.
For a button inside a field, use size.control.compact. Don't use size.control.default. A clear or step button fits inside the field, so the field keeps its row height.
Button's default size. Actions outside tables: forms, dialogs, page actions.
Button's compact size. Table rows and toolbars. Compact still fits a mouse.
Button's large size isn't used. Controls stay small so more records fit on one screen.
Input group's block-start align isn't used. Inputs stay one line high in toolbars and filter bars.
Input group's block-end align isn't used. Inputs stay one line high in toolbars and filter bars.
Field's horizontal orientation. Settings and filter panels: switches and short controls with the label beside.
Sidebar's lg size isn't used. Rows stay small so the whole navigation fits the screen all shift.
Toggle's default size isn't used. Toggles sit in the table toolbar, at the smaller size like compact buttons.
Toggle's sm size. The table toolbar, matching compact buttons. It still fits a mouse.
Toggle's lg size isn't used. Controls stay small so more records fit on one screen.

why: radius.2: We use a 2px corner for buttons and inputs in order to mark their role as controls and keep density. A small radius does this by softening the edge just enough to read as an object, while it keeps straight lines that align in rows. So a dense toolbar reads as one line of actions, because the product is dense (content.q2) and precise (brand.q1), with slightly rounded controls (shape.values).

radius.2: We use the 2px control corner for boxes that grow in order to keep their role, as objects of one family, by inheritance from the control corner. The same radius does this by giving a list row or a text area the curve of the controls beside it. So rows and fields read as one family, because the control corner is small, not a pill (shape.values), and the product is dense (content.q2).

items.text: For an error message, use color.status.danger with an icon. Don't use color.status.warning. Red always means fix this, and the icon says it without color.
For the action that completes the task, use button primary, one per view. Don't use two primaries side by side. One primary makes the committing action obvious.
For a delete or remove, use button secondary, then confirm in a dialog with Button danger. Don't use button primary as the first step. Deleting is rare and costly; a confirm step catches mistakes.
For a confirmation question, use name the exact object and the consequence. Don't use "Are you sure?". Acting on the wrong record is the costly mistake.

items.text: For an option in a menu or list, use radius.option. Don't use radius.control. Options sit square inside the menu. A long list scans as one clean column.
For a something that grows past one line, use radius.element. Don't use radius.surface. Rows and text areas keep the small control corner, so long lists stay straight.
For a corners of cards, menus and dialogs, use radius.surface. Don't use radius.control. Cards and menus get a corner just softer than controls. Panels still tile neatly on a busy screen.

why: radius.2: We use a 2px corner for buttons and inputs in order to mark their role as controls and keep density. A small radius does this by softening the edge just enough to read as an object, while it keeps straight lines that align in rows. So a dense toolbar reads as one line of actions, because the product is dense (content.q2) and precise (brand.q1), with slightly rounded controls (shape.values).

radius.0: We use a square corner for menu options in order to keep nesting by the relation: the 4px surface corner minus the panel's 4px padding. The inner radius does this by following the outer curve at the padding's distance, and here no curve is left. So an option's edge runs parallel to its menu's edge, because surfaces take 4px (shape.roles, brand.q1) and the layout is compact (spacing.values).

radius.2: We use the 2px control corner for boxes that grow in order to keep their role, as objects of one family, by inheritance from the control corner. The same radius does this by giving a list row or a text area the curve of the controls beside it. So rows and fields read as one family, because the control corner is small, not a pill (shape.values), and the product is dense (content.q2).

radius.4: We use a 4px corner for cards, menus and dialogs in order to make touching panels read as separate objects, in a precise tone by brand convention. A small radius does this by breaking the outline at each corner, just softer than the 2px controls. So panels read apart yet still tile neatly, because containers get their own corner (shape.roles, shape.count) and the brand is precise (brand.q1).

brand-q3.why: IBM Plex Sans for every text role and IBM Plex Mono for data: exact and quiet, so the numbers stay the hero.

items.label: Readability
items.text: Plex Sans is a neutral grotesque with open shapes, made for screens; it reads at the small body size dense rows need.

items.label: Legibility
items.text: Data, codes and IDs sit in Plex Mono, where each character holds its own fixed cell, so they read character by character.

items.label: Scalability
items.text: Plex ships a full range of weights, so every role in the type scale has its own weight without a second sans.

items.label: Numerals
items.text: Digits in Plex Mono are all one width, so columns of numbers line up.

items.label: Scripts and languages
items.text: Plex Sans covers Latin, Cyrillic and Greek; Hebrew, Arabic and other scripts come as sister families of IBM Plex, drawn to match.

items.label: Recognition
items.text: One family with a matching mono gives the product an engineered, consistent voice.

items.label: Familiarity
items.text: A grotesque reads as standard and trusted in operations tools.

items.label: Personality
items.text: Precise, as the brand answer asks, and quiet, so the brand steps back.

items.label: Performance
items.text: Two families; load only the weights the scale uses.

items.label: Licensing
items.text: SIL Open Font License: free to embed in apps and on the web.

items.label: Fallback and pairing
items.text: Falls back to system-ui and ui-monospace, as its tokens say; Plex Mono is its own pair.

why: neutral.0, the same as content (surface.default): a menu stands out by its edge and its one shadow, not by its fill.
black.light.scrim: a see-through layer that dims the page behind a modal, so the dialog is the one thing to act on.

shadow.none: We use no shadow for cards in order to keep them at the page's height: on the scale only floating layers rise. The missing shade does this by leaving the card flat, framed by its line. So the page reads as one flat grid, because only menus and dialogs float (elevation.roles) and shadows are subtle (elevation.values).

shadow.overlay: We use step 2 of the shadow scale for menus and dialogs in order to show their height as floating layers. The cast shade does this by an 8px offset and a 24px blur at 16% under the panel's edge. So a menu reads as above the grid without a heavy edge, because only what floats rises (elevation.roles) and shadows are subtle (elevation.values).
neutral.50, the same as content (surface.default): a menu stands out by its edge and its one shadow, not by its fill, as in light.
black.dark.scrim: a see-through layer that dims the page behind a modal, so the dialog is the one thing to act on.

shadow.overlay-dark: We use the light shadow's shape for menus and dialogs in dark in order to show the same floating height by the dark-shade relation. The cast shade does this by the same 8px offset and 24px blur, at 50% black instead of 16%. So a menu still lifts off the dark page, though its shade reads weaker on dark than in light, because only what floats rises (elevation.roles) and dark ships as standard (theming.values).

items.text: For a button label, use one verb from the word list. Don't use a sentence or "Please". Labels repeat on every screen; one verb reads fastest.
